analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Jones Act so foreign-built and foreign-operated ships can carry goods between U.S. ports.
analysis.headline: Introduced with no cosponsors, the Jones Act repeal bill has sat in the Senate Commerce Committee since June 2025 with no hearing and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Jones Act, shipping goods between U.S. ports is restricted to vessels built in the United States, owned by U.S. citizens, and mostly crewed by Americans. This bill would erase that restriction, allowing any vessel legally registered in the U.S. to carry cargo coastwise, with the Coast Guard directed to issue safety and security rules within 90 days. Supporters argue the protection raises shipping costs that consumers pay, especially in Puerto Rico, Hawaii, and Alaska; opponents argue it would wipe out the U.S. merchant fleet and the shipyards that depend on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and businesses that pay shipping costs on goods moving between U.S. ports — especially households and importers in Puerto Rico, Hawaii, Alaska, and other non-contiguous places, where the Jones Act's protected rates are highest. Foreign vessel operators would also gain access to the domestic market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers in Puerto Rico, Hawaii, and Alaska

how_it_helps.text: The bill rewrites federal shipping law so a coastwise endorsement can go to any vessel qualified under U.S. law to engage in coastwise trade, ending the requirement that ships be U.S.-built [S2].

It repeals or conforms a series of related restrictions, including rules on tank vessels, liquified gas tankers, small passenger vessels, and penalties that strip coastwise privileges, opening the domestic shipping market to competition [S2].
The Coast Guard would be required to issue regulations within 90 days requiring all newly eligible vessels to meet the same safety and security requirements [S2].

analysis.who_pays: U.S.-flag shipping companies and American shipyard workers. The U.S.-built, U.S.-flagged, U.S.-crewed requirements are what protect the domestic fleet and shipyards from foreign competition; repeal removes that captive market, putting U.S. mariner jobs and shipyard orders at risk. National security officials and the industry have long argued the protected fleet is a wartime asset.
analysis.who_pays_short: U.S. shipping firms and shipyard workers

drawbacks.text: Repeal would expose the U.S. fleet and shipyards to competition from foreign-built, foreign-staffed vessels, a structure that now exists because of the protections the bill strikes from title 46 of the U.S. Code [S2].

The strongest good-faith objection: the Jones Act fleet is treated as a national security reserve of ships, crews, and shipbuilding capacity, and its supporters argue a large share of those jobs and that capacity would not survive open competition with lower-cost foreign operators — a cost the bill does not address beyond its safety-and-security regulations [S2].

Repeal also removes the legal penalty mechanism (section 12132) under which vessels lose coastwise privileges, and strips the U.S.-qualification link from tanker and passenger-vessel rules, a wide technical rewrite some would argue deserves a fuller hearing than it has received [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains would flow to a broad but diffuse group — consumers and importers paying Jones Act shipping premiums — while the costs fall on a concentrated group of shipowners and shipyard workers who have been sheltered by the law for a century. That makes repeal economically appealing in aggregate but politically hard, and the bill offers nothing to cushion the job losses and industrial capacity at stake, which is a real weakness even for supporters of the policy.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it has drawn no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Lee introduced S. 2043, the Open America's Waters Act, on June 12, 2025 [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S4].
No other action has been taken, and the bill has zero cosponsors [S3], [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The U.S.-flag shipping industry and the shipyards that build for it, which keep the legal protection from foreign competition that the bill would have removed. sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no cosponsor signed on, so there is no record of how members split on the bill; Jones Act repeal has historically found only scattered support in both parties and strong opposition from the affected industry.

industries.note: The Jones Act guarantees that cargo moving between U.S. ports travels on U.S.-built, U.S.-owned, U.S.-crewed ships, letting these carriers charge rates far above foreign alternatives. Repeal would expose them to open competition, and their gain from protection comes directly out of consumers' pockets.

Domestic shipyards rely on the Jones Act's requirement that U.S.-trade ships be built in America, which gives them a captive market of coastal vessels. Repeal would remove that market and the shipyard and mariner jobs tied to it.

Foreign-built and foreign-staffed ships would gain legal access to the U.S. coastal cargo market. Their expansion is what lowers the shipping premiums that consumers, especially in Puerto Rico, Hawaii, and Alaska, currently pay.

analysis.trajectory: The 119th Congress is still in session, but a bill referred to committee with zero cosponsors and no committee action for months almost never reaches the floor. Absent a vehicle like a broader shipping bill to carry the idea, it is likely to die at the end of this Congress.
